newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI sets out blueprint for ECB policy tools.
newsitem.headline: EMI sets out blueprint for ECB policy tools.

text.p: The European Central Bank, responsible for monetary policy under a single currency, will mainly use open market operations but will also offer funds under two standing facilities, the European Monetary Institute said on Friday.

The Frankfurt-based forerunner to the ECB said in a report that it was also preparing the basis to allow the use of minimum reserves as an additional policy tool, but said the final decision on whether these would be used and what form they would take would be left to the ECB itself.

"The minimum reserve system which will also be made available may serve the purpose of stabilising money market interest rates, creating or enlarging a structural liquidity shortage in the money market and possibly contributing to the control of monetary expansion," the EMI said.

In preparation for the possible adoption of the reserve instrument, the EMI published a prepared proposal which would allow the European Union council to set up the legal basis for the use of the instrument.
It left open the question of whether or not the deposits with the central bank would bear interest.
The German central bank, which is one of the main advocates of the use of minimum reserves, requires funds to be held interest-free, a practice which is extremely unpopular with domestic banks.

In its only comment on the likelihood of the reserves bearing interest, the EMI said in an annex to the report, "If the ECB were to decide to remunerate minimum reserves, the rate of interest would be set according to a fixed formula related to a market or an official interest rate chosen by the ECB."
The EMI said that the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) would have four types of open market operations at its disposal.
Its main refinancing operations would be regular liquidity-providing reverse transactions, offered weekly, and with a maturity of two weeks.
Longer-term refinancing operations with a monthly frequency and a maturity of three months would also be offered to cater for a limited part of the global refinancing volume.

In addition, the ESCB would use fine-tuning operations and structural operations, the EMI said. As one means of affecting the structural liquidity position of the banking sector with regard to the ESCB, debt certificates could be issued.
These would be issued by the ECB in the form of a standard tender, the EMI said.
Two standing facilities would exist alongside the open market operations, forming the floor and ceiling for overnight funds rates, the report continued.
"Two standing facilities will be available to provide, in the case of the marginal lending facility, or to absorb, in the case of the desposit facility, overnight liquidity," the EMI said.
"These facilities will bound overnight market interest rates and the interest rates applied to them will help in signalling the general stance of monetary policy," it added.
